title: Nachiketa turns down the world
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: Nachiketa refuses Death's prizes; the Isha warns of people who forget the self
carry: the atman is worth more than the world
tomorrow: how can one thing move and not move at the same time?

cards: Scroll long enough and something is always for sale. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa gets the biggest offer anyone ever got. He's at the house of Yama, Death himself, and he's asked what happens to the self.
Yama tries to buy him off: sons and grandsons, herds and gold, horses, wide lands, a life as long as he likes. Nachiketa says: keep your horses, your songs and dances. Tell me about the self.
The Isha's third verse shows the other road.

teach.b: Asurya nama te loka andhena tamasavritah. Worlds known as sunless, covered in blind darkness. Who goes there?
One word answers: atmahano. Atman, self, and han, to strike. Self-slayers.
Shankara, the old commentator, reads it as people who live as if the deep self weren't there, who bury it under grabbing and forgetting. And the verse's last word is janah, people. Not monsters.
People who forgot. Here's the teaching.

teach.h: THE ATMAN: WORTH MORE THAN THE WORLD.
teach.b: The atman, the self, is the most precious thing in Hindu thought, and in Shankara's school it is one with Brahman, the ground of everything.
Nachiketa turned down the whole world to know it; the Isha warns about people who trade it away. A neighbor tradition asks almost the same question.

teach.h: MARK: GAIN THE WORLD, LOSE THE SOUL.
teach.b: In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus says: For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? Both warn you can win everything and lose the one doing the winning.
An honest difference: in Mark, the soul is a person's own life before God; in Shankara's reading, the atman is one with Brahman.
If the word self-slayers lands heavier than that today, 988 in the US, or local emergency help elsewhere, is there to call or text.

how: Hindu teachers who follow Shankara read this verse as a warning against ignoring the atman, not as a curse; it is often taught alongside Nachiketa's refusal of Death's gifts in the Katha Upanishad.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: the Isha in English, skipping the hard verses
a list of punishments after death
a boy who chose the self over everything Death offered

games.q: verse three, and a neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: self-slayers: those who forget the self
refused Death's gifts to know the self
gain the whole world, lose the soul

s: the Isha's 'self-slayers' verse is about taking one's own life
Shankara reads it as living as if the deep self weren't there.
the verse's last word is janah, people
Mark and the Isha mean the same thing by the self
they share a question; Mark's soul and Shankara's atman are understood differently.

games.q: a friend says, 'religions all say the same thing about the soul anyway.' you've just read Isha 3 and Mark 8:36. what's the fairest reply?
o: yes, they're the same teaching in two languages.
they share a warning, but they mean different things by the self.
no, they have nothing in common at all.
games.why: both warn you can win everything and lose the one doing the winning. Mark's soul answers to God; Shankara's atman is one with Brahman. alike, and honestly different.

practice: Close your eyes and let the dark behind the lids be only dark, nothing to fear. With each breath, notice the one who is noticing: still here, unhurt, not for sale.
When a thought tries to sell you something, let it pass, and come back to the one who noticed it.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verse three: worlds known as asurya, sunless, and atmahano, those who forget the self, while Nachiketa chose it over everything.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: atmahanah, self-slayers, from atman, self, and han, to strike.

carryVoice: Your line: the atman is worth more than the world. Nachiketa knew it. Rest well tonight.
